title: bs58 0.5.1: Base58 core and selected builder behavior in a proof fork
explanation:
bs58 converts byte sequences to Base58 symbols and back. This report describes contracts for an adapted proof fork of bs58 0.5.1. A fresh integrated verification checks the selected core functions, helpers and extension wrappers; the previously accepted core result is documented separately. The codec guarantees require a valid alphabet and disabled checksum checking.

The core encoder preserves the input's base-256 numeric value in base 58 and maps each leading zero byte to a leading zero symbol. The decoder preserves the numeric value in base 256 and maps each leading zero symbol to a zero byte. Each returns the exact output prefix and length if it fits, or `BufferTooSmall` otherwise. For invalid encoded input, the decoder reports the first non-ASCII byte index or the first invalid ASCII character and its index, unless an earlier valid prefix has already exceeded the output capacity, in which case it reports `BufferTooSmall` first. On success both leave the unused output suffix unchanged; errors do not promise rollback. The fixed-array decoder returns the decoded bytes padded with zeros, without requiring the decoded length to equal the array length. The four selected core functions terminate and satisfy their checked panic obligations within their modeled domains.

`Alphabet::new` accepts exactly distinct ASCII arrays of 58 bytes and otherwise identifies the first non-ASCII or duplicate byte with its specified indices and character. The selected runtime constructor and convenience contracts cover successful `new_unwrap` and the validity of BITCOIN, MONERO, RIPPLE, FLICKR and DEFAULT; MONERO and BITCOIN have equal tables, and DEFAULT is BITCOIN. The fixed-array unwrap requires successful decoding; invalid inputs deliberately panic.

For concrete byte-slice inputs and byte-slice targets (and the decoder’s array target), disabled-check builder operations carry the core result and mutation guarantees through the selected dispatch. The encoded length bound for input length `n` is `h(n) = n + floor((n + 1) / 2)`; evaluating it requires the intermediate and final machine additions to fit `usize`. Under the stock allocation model, with a valid alphabet and the stated machine addition bounds, the specialized growing-vector encoder appends the exact encoding and succeeds. The corresponding decoder appends the exact decoding on success; it cannot return `BufferTooSmall` for any input, although character errors remain possible. Both preserve the old vector prefix. On decode error the vector retains its enlarged length and the partially modified appended tail. The `into_vec` variants start empty and return the exact output on success.

The mathematical relations establish both round trips: decoding an encoding recovers the input bytes, and encoding a valid alphabet-only sequence after decoding recovers that sequence. A separate composed operation establishes the actual encoding-to-decoding vector round trip under its length and alphabet premises. Builder constructors and alphabet setters preserve their specified fields. In the full-feature state projection, checksum setters establish only the resulting mode and version fields. Selected error Clone and PartialEq behavior and Alphabet Clone are also covered by their contracts. See the [core specification](https://github.com/MasWag/crate-proofs/blob/66a831cffae94736ab5344af279329338a9e17ea/bs58/0.5.1/creusot/verification/specification.md) and [extension specification](https://github.com/MasWag/crate-proofs/blob/66a831cffae94736ab5344af279329338a9e17ea/bs58/0.5.1/creusot/verification/extensions/specification.md) for exact relations.
trusted_assumptions: The guarantees rely on the Rust compiler, Creusot translation and its shipped standard-library models, Why3 transformations, and SMT solvers. The selected extension uses unmodified standard models, with no trusted application algorithm or arithmetic lemma. Vector correctness relies on the modeled sequence behavior of `push`, `pop`, and range indexing; the checked loops preserve the specified byte contents and lengths. Physical capacity-limit panics, including Rust allocation-domain limits, and resource failures are outside these models.
limitations:
This is an adapted verification fork, not the unchanged release. The core specializes the generic encoder to byte slices and uses index loops, explicit reversal and bounded arithmetic expressions. The extension specializes inputs and targets and replaces vector resize and truncate with push-zero and pop loops, changing allocation strategy and cost. Vector guarantees cover byte contents and logical length and prefix; capacity, pointer identity, and allocation-call sequence are outside those claims. Its `onto_vec` adapters call the core directly on the appended tail rather than verifying generic Vec target dispatch. Source review and finite native comparisons support correspondence to the release, but there is no formal release-equivalence theorem. See [core correspondence](https://github.com/MasWag/crate-proofs/blob/66a831cffae94736ab5344af279329338a9e17ea/bs58/0.5.1/creusot/correspondence.md) and [extension correspondence](https://github.com/MasWag/crate-proofs/blob/66a831cffae94736ab5344af279329338a9e17ea/bs58/0.5.1/creusot/extensions/correspondence.md).

Generic target behavior is conditional on its callback contract; arbitrary legal targets need not invoke the callback. Arbitrary `AsRef` observations need not be stable. A conventional generic iterator guarantee requires a checked law that the original and cloned `IntoIterator` values produce identical finite sequences; `Clone + IntoIterator` alone does not establish it. The runtime fixed-array and alphabet proofs do not establish compiler constant-evaluation semantics. No blanket termination claim is made for the wrappers.

Checksum state updates do not prove digest computation or checked codec behavior. SHA calls lack the necessary contracts in the installed models. String construction and mutation, UTF-8 repair and the ASCII-to-byte bridge also lack the needed model relations; observable formatting is unmodeled. The observed [optional-container model gaps](https://github.com/MasWag/crate-proofs/blob/66a831cffae94736ab5344af279329338a9e17ea/bs58/0.5.1/creusot/verification/extensions/optional-boundaries.md) include calls used for SmallVec and tinyvec resizing and spare-slice access; their adapters are not covered. The report does not establish whole-crate undefined-behavior freedom, cryptographic properties, or string formatting. The existing findings concern separately reproduced checksum behavior. Details are in the [model boundaries](https://github.com/MasWag/crate-proofs/blob/66a831cffae94736ab5344af279329338a9e17ea/bs58/0.5.1/creusot/verification/extensions/model-boundaries.md).
environment:
The original accepted core proof used unmodified Creusot 0.13.0 on x86_64 Linux with its standard models; its [results](https://github.com/MasWag/crate-proofs/blob/66a831cffae94736ab5344af279329338a9e17ea/bs58/0.5.1/creusot/verification/results.md) describe that historical run. A fresh integrated run verified the selected core bodies, helpers and extension wrappers together using unmodified Creusot 0.13.0 and its standard models. A local checker audited trait goals and printer identity; it was reviewed and tested with negative controls and does not modify the verifier. A separate native comparison exercised the adapted implementation against the release, including complete modeled byte and error states; finite comparisons are not an equivalence theorem. The [extension results](https://github.com/MasWag/crate-proofs/blob/66a831cffae94736ab5344af279329338a9e17ea/bs58/0.5.1/creusot/verification/extensions/results.md) and [evidence summary](https://github.com/MasWag/crate-proofs/blob/66a831cffae94736ab5344af279329338a9e17ea/bs58/0.5.1/creusot/verification/extensions/evidence/summary.json) describe the fresh run, and [tool identities](https://github.com/MasWag/crate-proofs/blob/66a831cffae94736ab5344af279329338a9e17ea/bs58/0.5.1/creusot/verification/toolchain.json) document the toolchain.

The standard cargo-proofs recording imported panic-contract verification for 21 named fork functions, a subset of the selected coverage. The complete functional verification and inventory include the selected generic builder methods and trait refinements omitted from those API bindings. The bindings name functions from the verification fork; Rustdoc signatures and safety classifications were not independently imported. See the [recording receipt](https://github.com/MasWag/crate-proofs/blob/6b6b19d4b5dff668d9f35f4c6afacee87461bc55/bs58/0.5.1/creusot/extensions/publication/recorded-run-summary.json) for the recording and its scope.
